Skills-Checks (SC) nutrition
  • SC 1 children estimate how much they should drink per training session and check it (e.g. with markings on the water bottle).
  • SC 2 children independently check that all important items are packed (bag check).
  • SC Document and discuss one day of nutrition: food, drinks and snacks.
  • SC Independently put together a meal/snack for before, during and after training/competition and discuss it.
  • SC Experiment with different snacks, hydration strategies or meals before/during/after training/competition and adapt them individually.
  • SC 1 test nutrition and hydration under competition conditions (e.g. gels, isotonic drinks during exercise).
  • SC 2 document and analyse fluid loss, energy needs and recovery.
–

Joint snack preparation or cooking classes.

Goal

  • Basic understanding of balanced nutrition
  • Promote healthy everyday habits
  • Link between nutrition
  • energy for sport and school

Balanced diet

  • ½ vegetables/fruit
  • ¼ carbohydrates
  • ¼ protein at every meal

Drinking

  • Water as the main drink
  • approx
  • 1.5–2 l daily
  • more when training

Regular meals

  • Breakfast
  • lunch
  • dinner and 2 healthy snacks (e.g. fruit, nuts)

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Goal

Strengthen awareness and adaptation; deepen understanding of macronutrients (carbohydrates, protein, fat) and fluid needs.

Before training

  • Drink approx
  • 500 ml of water 1–2h beforehand
  • In heat or with high salt loss
  • use lightly salted drinks (1 pinch of salt)

During training

Drink 150–200 ml every 15–20'; for efforts >1h add carbohydrates (e.g. diluted fruit juices).

After training

  • 0.5-1 l of fluid within 30'
  • For intense efforts use electrolyte drinks or lightly salted water

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Balanced diet

Drinking

Regular meals

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Before training

  • 2–3h beforehand: carbohydrate-rich
  • easily digestible meal (e.g. wholegrain bread with honey)
  • 30' beforehand: small snack (e.g. banana)

During training (>1h exertion)

30–60 g of carbohydrates per hour (e.g. energy bar, dried fruit)

After training

Within 30': snack with carbohydrates and protein (e.g. yoghurt with fruit, milkshake).

Main meal

  • balanced with carbohydrates (e.g. rice, pasta)
  • protein (e.g. chicken, lentils) and vegetables

Skills-Checks (SC) sleep
  • SC Questions for the children: how many hours of sleep do we need? What helps us sleep better?
  • SC For one week, document sleep duration and how they feel the next day.
  • SC Try breathing techniques or progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) before sleep.
  • SC 1 document sleep duration and quality for one week, together with training performance.
  • SC 2 reflect on evening routines and make adjustments.
  • SC 1 create and implement a plan for sleep and meal times before a competition.
  • SC 2 "park" thoughts before sleep, e.g. by writing them down or with breathing exercises (rumination stop)
–
Sleep content

Sleep duration

8–10h/night
Sleep supports concentration, energy and recovery.

Sleep duration

8–10h/night

Routine

Same bedtimes, also at weekends.

Relaxation

  • Avoid screens 1h before sleep
  • introduce rituals such as reading or breathing exercises

Sleep environment

  • Dark
  • cool
  • quiet (16–18°C)
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Regular sleep times

Build in relaxation rituals

Rumination stop

  • Get up if awake for a long time
  • Write down thoughts to clear your head
  • Turn negative thoughts about sleep into positive beliefs

Optimised use of caffeine and aids

  • Consider the effect (half-life 6h, stronger effect in adolescents)
  • avoid at least 6h before sleep
  • Use eye masks
  • ear protection
  • etc

Plan power naps

  • Short naps of 10–15' for recovery
  • ideally after lunch

Adjustments for travel and competitions

  • Adapt sleep and meal times to time zone changes
  • Use strategies against jet lag
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Targeted and individual sleep optimisation secures long-term performance.

Regular sleep routines and adapting to travel or competitions are decisive.

  • Sleep problems should be monitored and treated if necessary
  • Power naps and relaxation techniques such as the rumination stop promote recovery and mental calm

Skills-Checks (SC) mental skills
  • SC Athletes talk about a moment they are proud of.
  • SC Athletes describe their emotions in difficult situations (e.g. after a mistake) using a traffic light.

Red

I am angry.

Yellow

I am unsure.

Green

I am calm/focused.

  • SC Athletes perform a task (e.g. technique exercise) with distractions (e.g. noise): test the ability to stay focused.
  • SC 1 Athletes formulate a small goal for training and explain why it matters to them.
  • SC 2 Simulated stress situation (e.g. competition simulation). Children consciously use techniques (e.g. breathing) to reach 'green'.
  • SC Athletes describe a best performance: 'How did you feel?': identify and apply the characteristics of the personal optimal performance state.
  • SC 1 for each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 during e.g. interval training, consciously use breathing techniques to stay calm.
  • SC 3 before a technique task, mentally rehearse the sequence.
  • SC 1 For each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 Use positive self-talk in a difficult task (e.g. time pressure).
  • SC 3 Perform a technique exercise with built-in distractions.

Static exercises

  • Hold static positions at maximum range of motion
  • After loading or in/as a training session (cool-down, yoga)

Training is adapted to the athletes' performance level and performance tests and split into upper body and lower body

  • Increase maximum strength through intramuscular coordination training of the upper and lower extremities (express muscle potential)

  • Core training

  • Maintain explosive and maximum strength
  • Adapting volume to competitions
  • Intensity remains

Technique – overarching

Discover, acquire and consolidate the basics of skiing:

  • parallel turns (skidded)
  • one-legged turns (easy terrain)
  • switch skiing in V position with changes of direction
  • skating step on the flat
  • waltz
  • playful learning through courses and free skiing
  • Free skiing: use every opportunity
Racing Konzept

Apply and vary the basics of skiing:

  • skiing in a defined space (pole forest)
  • parallel turns (skidded and carved)
  • short turns on an easy slope
  • one-legged turns on an easy slope
  • parallel turn switch (skidded)
  • efficient skating step
  • waltz
  • Basic Air (edge of slope)
  • playful learning through stations and free skiing
  • First runs in a kids cross
  • Free skiing: use every opportunity and experience basic technique
Racing Konzept

Acquire the specific basics (Racing Basics 1-3) of alpine skiing:

  • skiing in gates
  • • basic race turn
  • Short turns on a difficult slope
  • skiing on one ski without poles
  • acceleration through coordinated skating steps (start)
  • tuck jump

Acquire and consolidate general basics:

  • parallel turn switch
  • parallel turns in ungroomed snow
  • piste trick (180°, powerslide)
  • Basic Air (small kicker)
  • playful learning through stations and free skiing
  • Skiing in a kids cross
  • Free skiing: implement in training to apply basic technique
  • Use terrain and snow conditions for variation

Skills-Checks (SC) nutrition
  • SC 1 children estimate how much they should drink per training session and check it (e.g. with markings on the water bottle).
  • SC 2 children independently check that all important items are packed (bag check).
  • SC Document and discuss one day of nutrition: food, drinks and snacks.
  • SC Independently put together a meal/snack for before, during and after training/competition and discuss it.
  • SC Experiment with different snacks, hydration strategies or meals before/during/after training/competition and adapt them individually.
  • SC 1 test nutrition and hydration under competition conditions (e.g. gels, isotonic drinks during exercise).
  • SC 2 document and analyse fluid loss, energy needs and recovery.

Goal

Strengthen awareness and adaptation; deepen understanding of macronutrients (carbohydrates, protein, fat) and fluid needs.

Before training

  • Drink approx
  • 500 ml of water 1–2h beforehand
  • In heat or with high salt loss
  • use lightly salted drinks (1 pinch of salt)

During training

Drink 150–200 ml every 15–20'; for efforts >1h add carbohydrates (e.g. diluted fruit juices).

After training

  • 0.5-1 l of fluid within 30'
  • For intense efforts use electrolyte drinks or lightly salted water

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Goal

Balanced diet

  • ½ vegetables/fruit
  • ¼ carbohydrates
  • ¼ protein at every meal

Drinking

  • Water as the main drink
  • approx
  • 1.5–2 l daily
  • more when training

Regular meals

  • Breakfast
  • lunch
  • dinner and 2 healthy snacks (e.g. fruit, nuts)

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Before training

  • 2–3h beforehand: carbohydrate-rich
  • easily digestible meal (e.g. wholegrain bread with honey)
  • 30' beforehand: small snack (e.g. banana)

During training (>1h exertion)

30–60 g of carbohydrates per hour (e.g. energy bar, dried fruit)

After training

Within 30': snack with carbohydrates and protein (e.g. yoghurt with fruit, milkshake).

Main meal

  • balanced with carbohydrates (e.g. rice, pasta)
  • protein (e.g. chicken, lentils) and vegetables

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Skills-Checks (SC) sleep
  • SC Questions for the children: how many hours of sleep do we need? What helps us sleep better?
  • SC For one week, document sleep duration and how they feel the next day.
  • SC Try breathing techniques or progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) before sleep.
  • SC 1 document sleep duration and quality for one week, together with training performance.
  • SC 2 reflect on evening routines and make adjustments.
  • SC 1 create and implement a plan for sleep and meal times before a competition.
  • SC 2 "park" thoughts before sleep, e.g. by writing them down or with breathing exercises (rumination stop)

Coming soon…

Sleep content

Sleep duration

8–10h/night
Sleep supports concentration, energy and recovery.

Sleep duration

8–10h/night

Routine

Same bedtimes, also at weekends.

Relaxation

  • Avoid screens 1h before sleep
  • introduce rituals such as reading or breathing exercises

Sleep environment

  • Dark
  • cool
  • quiet (16–18°C)
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Regular sleep times

Build in relaxation rituals

Rumination stop

  • Get up if awake for a long time
  • Write down thoughts to clear your head
  • Turn negative thoughts about sleep into positive beliefs

Optimised use of caffeine and aids

  • Consider the effect (half-life 6h, stronger effect in adolescents)
  • avoid at least 6h before sleep
  • Use eye masks
  • ear protection
  • etc

Plan power naps

  • Short naps of 10–15' for recovery
  • ideally after lunch

Adjustments for travel and competitions

  • Adapt sleep and meal times to time zone changes
  • Use strategies against jet lag
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Targeted and individual sleep optimisation secures long-term performance.

Regular sleep routines and adapting to travel or competitions are decisive.

  • Sleep problems should be monitored and treated if necessary
  • Power naps and relaxation techniques such as the rumination stop promote recovery and mental calm

Skills-Checks (SC) mental skills
  • SC Athletes talk about a moment they are proud of.
  • SC Athletes describe their emotions in difficult situations (e.g. after a mistake) using a traffic light.

Red

I am angry.

Yellow

I am unsure.

Green

I am calm/focused.

  • SC Athletes perform a task (e.g. technique exercise) with distractions (e.g. noise): test the ability to stay focused.
  • SC 1 Athletes formulate a small goal for training and explain why it matters to them.
  • SC 2 Simulated stress situation (e.g. competition simulation). Children consciously use techniques (e.g. breathing) to reach 'green'.
  • SC Athletes describe a best performance: 'How did you feel?': identify and apply the characteristics of the personal optimal performance state.
  • SC 1 for each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 during e.g. interval training, consciously use breathing techniques to stay calm.
  • SC 3 before a technique task, mentally rehearse the sequence.
  • SC 1 For each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).

FTEM Kraft F3

Narrowing down

Playful forms of the basic movements: pushing, supporting, braking, pulling
Holistically strong

Preparation phase 1

  • Barbell technique with bodyweight and light additional loads (different squat forms)
  • First jump forms focusing on correct landing mechanisms (leg axis)
  • Developing core control and stability

Preparation phase 2

  • Increase strength potential
  • Increase explosive strength
  • Static core training with some dynamic forms

Pre-competition phase

  • Explosive strength training
  • Core training

Competition phase

  • Strength training with reduced volume
  • Maintain core training
  • Prevention programmes (ISPA)
FTEM Kraft T1FTEM Kraft T2

Loading

  • Develop strength using muscle strength exercises
  • Low to medium intensity with high training volume
  • Quality is decisive here
  • Technical development of the muscle strength exercises; with good quality
  • already work with additional loads

Preparation phase 1

  • Introduce the lower extremities and the core to the higher loads of the next stage
  • Technical development of barbell technique in the muscle power exercises

Preparation phase 2

  • Build muscle potential (use muscle strength exercises as training exercises)
  • Further develop and then use the muscle power exercises
  • Static and dynamic core training with additional loads
  • Explosive strength training with and without additional loads

Pre-competition phase

  • Increase maximum strength through intramuscular coordination training (express muscle potential)
  • Increase explosive strength with and without additional load
  • Include jump and landing variations
  • Include dynamic and static core strength in a polarised, sport-specific way

Competition phase

  • Maintain explosive and maximum strength
  • High intensities and reduced volume of strength sessions
  • Prevention programmes

Speed content

Start every training session with exercises from
the basic movement and game forms. These forms are cross-sport and promote children's movement competence.
Speed:
Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running,
jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping.

Explosiveness

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running, jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms
or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping

Make the basic game and movement forms joyful and
package them in imaginative, varied games.

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe F1&F2

Choose exercises from the basic movement and
game forms that accentuate one of the development factors
strength, explosiveness or speed.

Speed

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running,
jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping.

Explosiveness

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running, jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms
or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping

  • Make the basic game and movement forms joyful and package them in imaginative
  • varied games
Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe F1&F2

Choose exercises from the basic movement and
game forms that accentuate one of the development factors
strength, explosiveness or speed.

Speed

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running,
jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping.
Exercises from the basic athletic movements:
acceleration, being maximally fast or sprints with changes of direction.

Explosiveness

Exercises from the basic athletic movements
hopping/jumping, jumping/landing and throwing:
rope skipping, hoop jumps or throwing forms.

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe F3

Speed:

  • Acceleration
  • Maximum speed
  • Change of direction
  • from session to session, or plan two athletic forms in the same session.

Explosiveness

Start explosive strength training with 60-70% foundation training and 30-40% performance training, then gradually increase the share of performance training.
Performance training explosiveness: single before multiple jumps (e.g. two-leg jumps vertical and horizontal)
Foundation training explosiveness: increasing load tolerance, e.g. through different forms of rope skipping (thigh- or ankle-dominant, with partner, double jumps, etc.)

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T1

Increase the share of foundation training for explosiveness
and strength (at least 2/3), technical and athletic
foundation training to reduce load instead
of performance training (1/3).

Speed

Performance training speed: linear sprint training;
emphasis on training frequency speed
Foundation training speed: exercises for
movement control (technique training).

Explosiveness

In explosiveness training, increase the share of athletic and technical foundation training
Performance training explosiveness: single before multiple jumps (e.g. two-leg jumps vertical and horizontal)
Foundation training explosiveness: increasing load tolerance, e.g. through different forms of rope skipping

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T2

Speed:

  • Accelerations
  • Changes of direction
  • Maximum speed
  • Between individual sprints 1:10-20 rest (e.g. 5 sec sprint = at least 100 sec rest)
  • general:
  • Resistance pushing/pulling (accelerating)
  • Resistance pulling (transition phase)
  • Towing assistance (overspeed)

Explosiveness:

  • Develop jump forms
  • Performance training explosiveness: for jump forms, single before
  • multiple jumps (e.g. two-leg jumps vertical and horizontal)
Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T3

Speed:

  • Accelerations
  • Changes of direction
  • Maximum speed
  • Between individual sprints 1:10-20 rest (e.g. 5 sec sprint = at least 100 sec rest)
  • general:
  • Resistance pushing/pulling (accelerating)
  • Resistance pulling (transition phase)
  • Towing assistance (overspeed)

Explosiveness:

  • Develop jump forms
  • Development of jump forms across the entire force-velocity curve
  • Use of eccentric pre-stretching
  • Choose exercise forms that also target short braking and acceleration phases.
Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T4

Speed:

  • Accelerations
  • Changes of direction
  • Maximum speed
  • Between individual sprints 1:10-20 rest (e.g. 5 sec sprint = at least 100 sec rest)
  • general:
  • Resistance pushing/pulling (accelerating)
  • Resistance pulling (transition phase)
  • Towing assistance (overspeed)

Explosiveness:

  • Train jump forms that match the characteristics and load dynamics of the target form
  • Train jump forms across the entire force-velocity curve
  • Use of eccentric pre-stretching
  • Choose exercise forms that also target short braking and acceleration phases.

SelektionskonzeptSelektionsguideline

Home coach assessment

  • Prepared by the supporting organisation
  • Must be submitted on time via the assessment
  • AWK with the required weekly volumes (+/-)

The following test results must be available:

  • Power test
  • TCU
  • No results available = grade 1
  • Grading according to the percentages in the PISTE Guidelines

Competition results

  • The regional overall ranking U11/U13 of the respective interregional tour is used..
  • or the national overall ranking U15/U18 is used
  • The highest score from the possible disciplines is considered
  • Competition results must be available for a regional card
  • No competition results = grade 1
  • Grading according to the PISTE Guidelines
SelektionskonzeptSelektionsguideline

Home coach assessment

  • Prepared by the supporting organisation
  • Must be submitted on time via the assessment
  • AWK with the required weekly volumes (+/-)

The following test results must be available:

  • Power test
  • TCU on- and off-snow with values of at least 55% Performer or 75% Contender
  • No results available = grade 1
  • Grading according to the percentages in the PISTE Guidelines
  • For a national card, a national power test with an average of at least 51 points must be completed (from 26/27 with 55 pts)
  • Grading according to the percentages in the PISTE Guidelines

Competition results

  • The FIS/WSPL list is used
  • The highest score from the possible disciplines is considered
  • Grading according to the PISTE Guidelines (www.Thatsnowsports.ch)
  • Injury status must be justified with a medical certificate at the assessment

Preparation phase 1 (VP1): mid-May-Aug
–

Goals

  • make the musculature strong and resilient
  • Improve barbell technique
  • Develop a good aerobic base
  • Promote coordinative abilities
  • Variation of training methods

Content

  • strength endurance (light weights, high repetition count)
  • muscle building (moderate weights, approx. ten repetitions)
  • maximum strength training towards the end of this phase
  • Plyometrics (high repetition count)
  • Long
  • easy endurance sessions (cycling, running, inline)
  • Varied training focusing on coordination
  • strength and endurance
Preparation phase 2 (VP2): Sept-Oct
–

Goals

  • build speed
  • speed strength and explosive strength
  • Transfer base endurance into intensive interval forms
  • balance between recovery and load

Content

  • sprint forms
  • plyometrics (jump forms, low repetition count)
  • strength building (high weights, medium to low repetition counts)
  • interval runs and base endurance
  • deliberately include recovery phases
Pre-competition phase (VWP): Nov
–

Goals

  • maintain speed and explosive strength
  • Use snow training for the coordinative implementation of conditioning abilities
  • Stay healthy and mentally strong

Content

  • snow training with a high volume of training runs
  • Competition simulations
  • Focus on coolness and precision
  • Base endurance for recovery
  • Maintenance strength training
Competition phase (WP): Dec-Apr
–

Goals

  • competitions steer the training
  • Prioritise competitions (important, medium, minor)
  • Plan training blocks with recovery in mind
  • maintain strength and speed training
  • balance recovery and load

Content

  • targeted competition preparation
  • Strength and speed training
  • Clear recovery phases

Skills-Checks (SC) nutrition
  • SC 1 children estimate how much they should drink per training session and check it (e.g. with markings on the water bottle).
  • SC 2 children independently check that all important items are packed (bag check).
  • SC Document and discuss one day of nutrition: food, drinks and snacks.
  • SC Independently put together a meal/snack for before, during and after training/competition and discuss it.
  • SC Experiment with different snacks, hydration strategies or meals before/during/after training/competition and adapt them individually.
  • SC 1 test nutrition and hydration under competition conditions (e.g. gels, isotonic drinks during exercise).
  • SC 2 document and analyse fluid loss, energy needs and recovery.
–

Goal

Balanced diet

  • ½ vegetables/fruit
  • ¼ carbohydrates
  • ¼ protein at every meal

Drinking

Regular meals

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Goal

Strengthen awareness and adaptation; deepen understanding of macronutrients (carbohydrates, protein, fat) and fluid needs.

Before training

  • Drink approx
  • 500 ml of water 1–2h beforehand
  • In heat or with high salt loss
  • use lightly salted drinks (1 pinch of salt)

During training

Drink 150–200 ml every 15–20'; for efforts >1h add carbohydrates (e.g. diluted fruit juices).

After training

  • 0.5-1 l of fluid within 30'
  • For intense efforts use electrolyte drinks or lightly salted water

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Balanced diet

Drinking

Regular meals

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Before training

  • 2–3h beforehand: carbohydrate-rich
  • easily digestible meal (e.g. wholegrain bread with honey)
  • 30' beforehand: small snack (e.g. banana)

During training (>1h exertion)

30–60 g of carbohydrates per hour (e.g. energy bar, dried fruit)

After training

Within 30': snack with carbohydrates and protein (e.g. yoghurt with fruit, milkshake).

Main meal

  • balanced with carbohydrates (e.g. rice, pasta)
  • protein (e.g. chicken, lentils) and vegetables

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Skills-Checks (SC) sleep
  • SC Questions for the children: how many hours of sleep do we need? What helps us sleep better?
  • SC For one week, document sleep duration and how they feel the next day.
  • SC Try breathing techniques or progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) before sleep.
  • SC 1 document sleep duration and quality for one week, together with training performance.
  • SC 2 reflect on evening routines and make adjustments.
  • SC 1 create and implement a plan for sleep and meal times before a competition.
  • SC 2 "park" thoughts before sleep, e.g. by writing them down or with breathing exercises (rumination stop)
–
Sleep content

Sleep duration

8–10h/night
Sleep supports concentration, energy and recovery.

Sleep duration

8–10h/night

Routine

Same bedtimes, also at weekends.

Relaxation

  • Avoid screens 1h before sleep
  • introduce rituals such as reading or breathing exercises

Sleep environment

  • Dark
  • cool
  • quiet (16–18°C)
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Regular sleep times

Build in relaxation rituals

Rumination stop

  • Get up if awake for a long time
  • Write down thoughts to clear your head
  • Turn negative thoughts about sleep into positive beliefs

Optimised use of caffeine and aids

  • Consider the effect (half-life 6h, stronger effect in adolescents)
  • avoid at least 6h before sleep
  • Use eye masks
  • ear protection
  • etc

Plan power naps

  • Short naps of 10–15' for recovery
  • ideally after lunch

Adjustments for travel and competitions

  • Adapt sleep and meal times to time zone changes
  • Use strategies against jet lag
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Targeted and individual sleep optimisation secures long-term performance.

Regular sleep routines and adapting to travel or competitions are decisive.

  • Sleep problems should be monitored and treated if necessary
  • Power naps and relaxation techniques such as the rumination stop promote recovery and mental calm

Skills-Checks (SC) mental skills
  • SC Athletes talk about a moment they are proud of.
  • SC Athletes describe their emotions in difficult situations (e.g. after a mistake) using a traffic light.

Red

I am angry.

Yellow

I am unsure.

Green

I am calm/focused.

  • SC Athletes perform a task (e.g. technique exercise) with distractions (e.g. noise): test the ability to stay focused.
  • SC 1 Athletes formulate a small goal for training and explain why it matters to them.
  • SC 2 Simulated stress situation (e.g. competition simulation). Children consciously use techniques (e.g. breathing) to reach 'green'.
  • SC Athletes describe a best performance: 'How did you feel?': identify and apply the characteristics of the personal optimal performance state.
  • SC 1 for each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 during e.g. interval training, consciously use breathing techniques to stay calm.
  • SC 3 before a technique task, mentally rehearse the sequence.
  • SC 1 For each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 Use positive self-talk in a difficult task (e.g. time pressure).
  • SC 3 Perform a technique exercise with built-in distractions.

  • Increase maximum strength through intramuscular coordination training of the upper and lower extremities (express muscle potential)
  • Training speed & explosive strength with and without additional load for the upper and lower extremities
  • Core training

  • Maintain explosive and maximum strength
  • Adapting volume to competitions
  • Intensity remains

Technique – overarching

Discover, acquire and consolidate the basics of alpine snowboarding:

  • basic turn (skidded)
  • one-foot riding on an easy slope (skidded)
  • switch riding with changes of direction on an easy slope (skidded)
  • waltz
  • playful learning through courses and free riding
Riding Konzept

Apply and vary the basics of alpine snowboarding:

  • riding in a defined space (pole forest, brooms etc.)
  • basic turn (skidded and carved)
  • short turns on an easy slope
  • one-foot riding on an easy slope (skidded and carved)
  • switch riding with changes of direction on an easy slope (skidded and carved)
  • waltz
  • Basic Air
  • playful learning through stations and free riding
Riding Konzept

Acquire the specific basics (Snowboard Alpin Essentials 1-):

  • Riding in gates
  • Basic race turn
  • Riding (short and long turns) on difficult slopes

Acquire and consolidate general basics:

  • riding on ungroomed slopes, • piste tricks (180°, Basic Air (small kicker), ollie, nollie, noserole, tailrole)
  • Playful learning through stations and free riding

Technique/tactics slalom

Basic Turn

Basic Turn (front & back side)

Steering phase 1 skidded

Steering phase 2 almost carved

carved turns

  • Consciously time-separated reducing, changing and increasing edge grip
  • Consciously release late to ride "straight" for a long time
  • Alternating loading and unloading in the turn
  • Pumping when riding roller turns (see roller track)
  • Terrain transitions without active flexing or extending: only movement forwards
  • Pressing terrain transitions: active flexing movement forwards - down
  • Terrain transitions with active take-off: active extending movement forwards - up
  • Pre-jumping terrain transitions: active pre-jump followed by active flexing movement forwards - down

Preparation phase 1 (VP1): mid-May-Aug
–

Goals

  • make the musculature strong and resilient
  • Improve barbell technique
  • Develop a good aerobic base
  • Promote coordinative abilities
  • Variation of training methods

Content

  • strength endurance (light weights, high repetition count)
  • muscle building (moderate weights, approx. ten repetitions)
  • maximum strength training towards the end of this phase
  • Plyometrics (high repetition count)
  • Long
  • easy endurance sessions (cycling, running, inline)
  • Varied training focusing on coordination
  • strength and endurance
Preparation phase 2 (VP2): Sept-Oct

100501

–

Goals

  • build speed
  • speed strength and explosive strength
  • Transfer base endurance into intensive interval forms
  • balance between recovery and load

Content

  • sprint forms
  • plyometrics (jump forms, low repetition count)
  • strength building (high weights, medium to low repetition counts)
  • interval runs and base endurance
  • deliberately include recovery phases
Pre-competition phase (VWP): Nov
–

Goals

  • maintain speed and explosive strength
  • Use snow training for the coordinative implementation of conditioning abilities
  • Stay healthy and mentally strong

Content

  • snow training with a high volume of training runs
  • Competition simulations
  • Focus on coolness and precision
  • Base endurance for recovery
  • Maintenance strength training
Competition phase (WP): Dec-Apr
–

Goals

  • competitions steer the training
  • Prioritise competitions (important, medium, minor)
  • Plan training blocks with recovery in mind
  • maintain strength and speed training
  • balance recovery and load

Content

  • targeted competition preparation
  • Strength and speed training
  • Clear recovery phases

Skills-Checks (SC) nutrition
  • SC 1 children estimate how much they should drink per training session and check it (e.g. with markings on the water bottle).
  • SC 2 children independently check that all important items are packed (bag check).
  • SC Document and discuss one day of nutrition: food, drinks and snacks.
  • SC Independently put together a meal/snack for before, during and after training/competition and discuss it.
  • SC Experiment with different snacks, hydration strategies or meals before/during/after training/competition and adapt them individually.
  • SC 1 test nutrition and hydration under competition conditions (e.g. gels, isotonic drinks during exercise).
  • SC 2 document and analyse fluid loss, energy needs and recovery.

Balanced diet

  • ½ vegetables/fruit
  • ¼ carbohydrates
  • ¼ protein at every meal

Drinking

  • Water as the main drink
  • approx
  • 1.5–2 l daily
  • more when training

Regular meals

  • Breakfast
  • lunch
  • dinner and 2 healthy snacks (e.g. fruit, nuts)

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Goal

Strengthen awareness and adaptation; deepen understanding of macronutrients (carbohydrates, protein, fat) and fluid needs.

Before training

  • Drink approx
  • 500 ml of water 1–2h beforehand
  • In heat or with high salt loss
  • use lightly salted drinks (1 pinch of salt)

During training

Drink 150–200 ml every 15–20'; for efforts >1h add carbohydrates (e.g. diluted fruit juices).

After training

  • 0.5-1 l of fluid within 30'
  • For intense efforts use electrolyte drinks or lightly salted water

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Balanced diet

Drinking

  • approx

Regular meals

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Before training

  • 2–3h beforehand: carbohydrate-rich
  • easily digestible meal (e.g. wholegrain bread with honey)
  • 30' beforehand: small snack (e.g. banana)

During training (>1h exertion)

30–60 g of carbohydrates per hour (e.g. energy bar, dried fruit)

After training

Within 30': snack with carbohydrates and protein (e.g. yoghurt with fruit, milkshake).

Main meal

  • balanced with carbohydrates (e.g. rice, pasta)
  • protein (e.g. chicken, lentils) and vegetables

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Skills-Checks (SC) sleep
  • SC Questions for the children: how many hours of sleep do we need? What helps us sleep better?
  • SC For one week, document sleep duration and how they feel the next day.
  • SC Try breathing techniques or progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) before sleep.
  • SC 1 document sleep duration and quality for one week, together with training performance.
  • SC 2 reflect on evening routines and make adjustments.
  • SC 1 create and implement a plan for sleep and meal times before a competition.
  • SC 2 "park" thoughts before sleep, e.g. by writing them down or with breathing exercises (rumination stop)
–
Sleep content

Sleep duration

8–10h/night
Sleep supports concentration, energy and recovery.

Sleep duration

8–10h/night

Routine

Same bedtimes, also at weekends.

Relaxation

  • Avoid screens 1h before sleep
  • introduce rituals such as reading or breathing exercises

Sleep environment

  • Dark
  • cool
  • quiet (16–18°C)
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Regular sleep times

Build in relaxation rituals

Rumination stop

  • Get up if awake for a long time
  • Write down thoughts to clear your head
  • Turn negative thoughts about sleep into positive beliefs

Optimised use of caffeine and aids

  • Consider the effect (half-life 6h, stronger effect in adolescents)
  • avoid at least 6h before sleep
  • Use eye masks
  • ear protection
  • etc

Plan power naps

  • Short naps of 10–15' for recovery
  • ideally after lunch

Adjustments for travel and competitions

  • Adapt sleep and meal times to time zone changes
  • Use strategies against jet lag
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Targeted and individual sleep optimisation secures long-term performance.

Regular sleep routines and adapting to travel or competitions are decisive.

  • Sleep problems should be monitored and treated if necessary
  • Power naps and relaxation techniques such as the rumination stop promote recovery and mental calm

Green

I am calm/focused.

  • SC Athletes perform a task (e.g. technique exercise) with distractions (e.g. noise): test the ability to stay focused.
  • SC 1 Athletes formulate a small goal for training and explain why it matters to them.
  • SC 2 Simulated stress situation (e.g. competition simulation). Children consciously use techniques (e.g. breathing) to reach 'green'.
  • SC Athletes describe a best performance: 'How did you feel?': identify and apply the characteristics of the personal optimal performance state.
  • SC 1 for each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 during e.g. interval training, consciously use breathing techniques to stay calm.
  • SC 3 before a technique task, mentally rehearse the sequence.
  • SC 1 For each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 Use positive self-talk in a difficult task (e.g. time pressure).
  • SC 3 Perform a technique exercise with built-in distractions.

  • Adapting volume to competitions
  • Intensity remains

Skills-Checks (SC) nutrition
  • SC 1 children estimate how much they should drink per training session and check it (e.g. with markings on the water bottle).
  • SC 2 children independently check that all important items are packed (bag check).
  • SC Document and discuss one day of nutrition: food, drinks and snacks.
  • SC Independently put together a meal/snack for before, during and after training/competition and discuss it.
  • SC Experiment with different snacks, hydration strategies or meals before/during/after training/competition and adapt them individually.
  • SC 1 test nutrition and hydration under competition conditions (e.g. gels, isotonic drinks during exercise).
  • SC 2 document and analyse fluid loss, energy needs and recovery.

Balanced diet

Preparation

Goal

Strengthen awareness and adaptation; deepen understanding of macronutrients (carbohydrates, protein, fat) and fluid needs.

Before training

  • Drink approx
  • 500 ml of water 1–2h beforehand
  • In heat or with high salt loss
  • use lightly salted drinks (1 pinch of salt)

During training

Drink 150–200 ml every 15–20'; for efforts >1h add carbohydrates (e.g. diluted fruit juices).

After training

  • 0.5-1 l of fluid within 30'
  • For intense efforts use electrolyte drinks or lightly salted water

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Goal

  • Promote healthy everyday habits

Balanced diet

  • ½ vegetables/fruit
  • ¼ carbohydrates
  • ¼ protein at every meal

Drinking

  • Water as the main drink
  • approx
  • 1.5–2 l daily

Regular meals

Preparation

Bring snacks and water bottle to training.

Before training

  • 2–3h beforehand: carbohydrate-rich
  • easily digestible meal (e.g. wholegrain bread with honey)
  • 30' beforehand: small snack (e.g. banana)

During training (>1h exertion)

30–60 g of carbohydrates per hour (e.g. energy bar, dried fruit)

After training

Within 30': snack with carbohydrates and protein (e.g. yoghurt with fruit, milkshake).

Main meal

  • balanced with carbohydrates (e.g. rice, pasta)
  • protein (e.g. chicken, lentils) and vegetables

Optimisation and individualisation

Advanced knowledge of micronutrients (vitamins, minerals) and their role in performance.

Skills-Checks (SC) sleep
  • SC Questions for the children: how many hours of sleep do we need? What helps us sleep better?
  • SC For one week, document sleep duration and how they feel the next day.
  • SC Try breathing techniques or progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) before sleep.
  • SC 1 document sleep duration and quality for one week, together with training performance.
  • SC 2 reflect on evening routines and make adjustments.
  • SC 1 create and implement a plan for sleep and meal times before a competition.
  • SC 2 "park" thoughts before sleep, e.g. by writing them down or with breathing exercises (rumination stop)

Coming soon…

Sleep content

Sleep duration

8–10h/night
Sleep supports concentration, energy and recovery.

Sleep duration

8–10h/night

Routine

Same bedtimes, also at weekends.

Relaxation

  • Avoid screens 1h before sleep
  • introduce rituals such as reading or breathing exercises

Sleep environment

  • Dark
  • cool
  • quiet (16–18°C)
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Regular sleep times

Build in relaxation rituals

Rumination stop

  • Get up if awake for a long time
  • Write down thoughts to clear your head
  • Turn negative thoughts about sleep into positive beliefs

Optimised use of caffeine and aids

  • Consider the effect (half-life 6h, stronger effect in adolescents)
  • avoid at least 6h before sleep
  • Use eye masks
  • ear protection
  • etc

Plan power naps

  • Short naps of 10–15' for recovery
  • ideally after lunch

Adjustments for travel and competitions

  • Adapt sleep and meal times to time zone changes
  • Use strategies against jet lag
Gesundheit & Entwicklung

Targeted and individual sleep optimisation secures long-term performance.

Regular sleep routines and adapting to travel or competitions are decisive.

  • Sleep problems should be monitored and treated if necessary
  • Power naps and relaxation techniques such as the rumination stop promote recovery and mental calm

Skills-Checks (SC) mental skills
  • SC Athletes talk about a moment they are proud of.
  • SC Athletes describe their emotions in difficult situations (e.g. after a mistake) using a traffic light.

Red

I am angry.

Yellow

I am unsure.

Green

I am calm/focused.

  • SC Athletes perform a task (e.g. technique exercise) with distractions (e.g. noise): test the ability to stay focused.
  • SC 1 Athletes formulate a small goal for training and explain why it matters to them.
  • SC 2 Simulated stress situation (e.g. competition simulation). Children consciously use techniques (e.g. breathing) to reach 'green'.
  • SC Athletes describe a best performance: 'How did you feel?': identify and apply the characteristics of the personal optimal performance state.
  • SC 1 for each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 during e.g. interval training, consciously use breathing techniques to stay calm.
  • SC 3 before a technique task, mentally rehearse the sequence.
  • SC 1 For each category, process goals and ranking goals (evaluate and adjust later).
  • SC 2 Use positive self-talk in a difficult task (e.g. time pressure).
  • SC 3 Perform a technique exercise with built-in distractions.

Endurance content

Playful endurance forms

Preparation phase 1

  • Base endurance

Preparation phase 2

  • Base endurance
  • Interval forms (VO2max)

Pre-competition phase

  • Interval forms (VO2max)
  • Base endurance as recovery

Competition phase

  • Base endurance for recovery
  • Maintain an active daily life and build load tolerance in the aerobic and especially the anaerobic range
  • Playful forms are recommended

Game forms:

  • Relays, fartlek
  • Small-sided games
  • Hidden (playful) intervals

How:

  • Variation of training means
  • Intensity above 80% HRmax
  • Free play time
  • Deliberately build in many short breaks

  • Intensive and extensive intervals
  • Repeated sprints
  • Small-sided games

Continuous steady load at moderate intensity, for example

HIIT or small-sided games

Narrowing down

Playful forms of the basic movements: pushing, supporting, braking, pulling
Holistically strong

Preparation phase 1

  • Barbell technique with bodyweight and light additional loads (different squat forms)
  • First jump forms focusing on correct landing mechanisms (leg axis)
  • Developing core control and stability

Preparation phase 2

  • Increase strength potential
  • Increase explosive strength
  • Static core training with some dynamic forms

Pre-competition phase

  • Explosive strength training
  • Core training

Competition phase

  • Strength training with reduced volume
  • Maintain core training
  • Prevention programmes (ISPA)
FTEM Kraft T1FTEM Kraft T2

Loading

  • Develop strength using muscle strength exercises
  • Low to medium intensity with high training volume
  • Quality is decisive here
  • Technical development of the muscle strength exercises; with good quality
  • already work with additional loads

Preparation phase 1

  • Introduce the lower extremities and the core to the higher loads of the next stage
  • Technical development of barbell technique in the muscle power exercises

Preparation phase 2

  • Build muscle potential (use muscle strength exercises as training exercises)
  • Further develop and then use the muscle power exercises
  • Static and dynamic core training with additional loads
  • Explosive strength training with and without additional loads

Pre-competition phase

  • Increase maximum strength through intramuscular coordination training (express muscle potential)
  • Increase explosive strength with and without additional load
  • Include jump and landing variations
  • Include dynamic and static core strength in a polarised, sport-specific way

Competition phase

  • Maintain explosive and maximum strength
  • High intensities and reduced volume of strength sessions
  • Prevention programmes

Speed content

Start every training session with exercises from
the basic movement and game forms. These forms are cross-sport and promote children's movement competence.
Speed:
Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running,
jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping.

Explosiveness

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running, jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms
or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping

Make the basic game and movement forms joyful and
package them in imaginative, varied games.

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe F1&F2

Choose exercises from the basic movement and
game forms that accentuate one of the development factors
strength, explosiveness or speed.

Speed

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running,
jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping.

Explosiveness

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running, jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms
or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping

  • Make the basic game and movement forms joyful and package them in imaginative
  • varied games
Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe F1&F2

Choose exercises from the basic movement and
game forms that accentuate one of the development factors
strength, explosiveness or speed.

Speed

Exercises from the basic movement and game forms to increase explosiveness: running,
jumping, hopping and jumping forms packaged in game forms or exercise forms to improve coordinative competence, throwing and catching, rope skipping.
Exercises from the basic athletic movements:
acceleration, being maximally fast or sprints with changes of direction.

Explosiveness

Exercises from the basic athletic movements
hopping/jumping, jumping/landing and throwing:
rope skipping, hoop jumps or throwing forms.

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe F3

Speed:

  • Acceleration
  • Maximum speed
  • Change of direction
  • from session to session, or plan two athletic forms in the same session.

Explosiveness

Start explosive strength training with 60-70% foundation training and 30-40% performance training, then gradually increase the share of performance training.
Performance training explosiveness: single before multiple jumps (e.g. two-leg jumps vertical and horizontal)
Foundation training explosiveness: increasing load tolerance, e.g. through different forms of rope skipping (thigh- or ankle-dominant, with partner, double jumps, etc.)

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T1

Increase the share of foundation training for explosiveness
and strength (at least 2/3), technical and athletic
foundation training to reduce load instead
of performance training (1/3).

Speed

Performance training speed: linear sprint training;
emphasis on training frequency speed
Foundation training speed: exercises for
movement control (technique training).

Explosiveness

In explosiveness training, increase the share of athletic and technical foundation training
Performance training explosiveness: single before multiple jumps (e.g. two-leg jumps vertical and horizontal)
Foundation training explosiveness: increasing load tolerance, e.g. through different forms of rope skipping

Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T2

Speed:

  • Accelerations
  • Changes of direction
  • Maximum speed
  • Between individual sprints 1:10-20 rest (e.g. 5 sec sprint = at least 100 sec rest)
  • general:
  • Resistance pushing/pulling (accelerating)
  • Resistance pulling (transition phase)
  • Towing assistance (overspeed)

Explosiveness:

  • Develop jump forms
  • Performance training explosiveness: for jump forms, single before
  • multiple jumps (e.g. two-leg jumps vertical and horizontal)
Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T3

Speed:

  • Accelerations
  • Changes of direction
  • Maximum speed
  • Between individual sprints 1:10-20 rest (e.g. 5 sec sprint = at least 100 sec rest)
  • general:
  • Resistance pushing/pulling (accelerating)
  • Resistance pulling (transition phase)
  • Towing assistance (overspeed)

Explosiveness:

  • Develop jump forms
  • Development of jump forms across the entire force-velocity curve
  • Use of eccentric pre-stretching
  • Choose exercise forms that also target short braking and acceleration phases.
Schnelligkeit Park& Pipe T4

Speed:

  • Accelerations
  • Changes of direction
  • Maximum speed
  • Between individual sprints 1:10-20 rest (e.g. 5 sec sprint = at least 100 sec rest)
  • general:
  • Resistance pushing/pulling (accelerating)
  • Resistance pulling (transition phase)
  • Towing assistance (overspeed)

Explosiveness:

  • Train jump forms that match the characteristics and load dynamics of the target form
  • Train jump forms across the entire force-velocity curve
  • Use of eccentric pre-stretching
  • Choose exercise forms that also target short braking and acceleration phases.

SelektionskonzeptSelektionsguideline

Home coach assessment

  • Prepared by the supporting organisation
  • Must be submitted on time via the assessment
  • AWK with the required weekly volumes (+/-)

The following test results must be available:

  • Power test
  • TCU
  • No results available = grade 1
  • Grading according to the percentages in the PISTE Guidelines

Competition results

  • The regional overall ranking U11/U13 of the respective interregional tour is used..
  • or the national overall ranking U15/U18 is used
  • The highest score from the possible disciplines is considered
  • Competition results must be available for a regional card
  • No competition results = grade 1
  • Grading according to the PISTE Guidelines
SelektionskonzeptSelektionsguideline

Home coach assessment

  • Prepared by the supporting organisation
  • Must be submitted on time via the assessment
  • AWK with the required weekly volumes (+/-)

The following test results must be available:

  • Power test
  • TCU on- and off-snow with values of at least 55% Performer or 75% Contender
  • No results available = grade 1
  • Grading according to the percentages in the PISTE Guidelines
  • For a national card, a national power test with an average of at least 51 points must be completed (from 26/27 with 55 pts)
  • Grading according to the percentages in the PISTE Guidelines

Competition results

  • The FIS/WSPL list is used
  • The highest score from the possible disciplines is considered
  • Grading according to the PISTE Guidelines (www.Thatsnowsports.ch)
  • Injury status must be justified with a medical certificate at the assessment
